prompt: What is the NIS2 directive and who does it apply to?
completion:
## NIS2 Directive – What it is **NIS2** (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) is the European Union’s second “Network and Information Security” directive. It replaces the original **NIS Directive (2016/1148)** and expands, strengthens and modernises the EU’s cyber‑security framework to cope with the current threat landscape. | Feature | Details | |---------|---------| | **Full title** | *Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (NIS2)* | | **Entry into force** | 17 Feb 2023 (member‑state transposition deadline 17 Feb 2025) | | **Purpose** | 1. Raise a **high common level of cybersecurity** across the Union. 2. Reduce fragmentation and improve cooperation among member‑states. 3. Protect critical infrastructure and digital services that are essential to the economy and society. | | **Scope of obligations** | • Risk‑management & security governance
• Incident‑reporting (within 24 h of detection)
• Supply‑chain & third‑party risk management
• Regular security audits
• Cooperation with EU & national authorities (EU‑NIS‑CSIRT, national CSIRTs, etc.) | --- ## Who does NIS2 apply to? ### 1. “Essential” and “Important” entities NIS2 introduces a **two‑tiered system** of applicability that applies to both **essential** and **important** entities (formerly “operators of essential services” only). | Tier | What it covers | Typical sectors & examples | |------|----------------|---------------------------| | **Essential** | Services that are crucial for the EU’s **economic, security, or societal functioning**. | Energy, transport (air, rail, road, maritime, water), banking & finance, health, drinking water, digital infrastructure (cloud, data centres, internet exchange points), critical public administration services. | | **Important** | Services that are **non‑essential but still important for the economy and society**. | Food, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, manufacturing, telecom (non‑critical), research & innovation, data‑processing, e‑commerce platforms, online marketplaces, social‑media, search engines, SaaS, cloud providers. | *The directive allows each member‑state to decide the **minimum thresholds** that determine whether an entity is “essential” or “important.”* Typical thresholds include turnover, number of employees, number of customers, and the nature of the service. ### 2. Digital Service Providers (DSPs) NIS2 adds a new **Digital Services Category** (a subset of “important” entities) that covers the **biggest and most influential online services**. | DSP category | Definition & examples | |--------------|-----------------------| | **Large DSPs** | Operators of **online marketplaces, social‑media platforms, search engines, cloud‑computing services, and online advertising services** that are **EU‑wide** or have a **significant user base** (e.g., > 20 million monthly active users, > €1 billion annual revenue). | | **Medium‑size DSPs** | Same services but with **lower thresholds** (e.g., > 10 million users or > €500 million revenue). | | **Small DSPs** | Operators that do not meet the above thresholds but still provide essential digital services (e.g., niche cloud services, regional marketplaces). | > **Key point:** All DSPs that fall under the thresholds must meet NIS2 obligations, regardless of whether they are located in the EU. Providers outside the EU that offer services to EU residents also fall under the scope. ### 3. Public Administration All **public bodies** that provide services covered by NIS2 are also subject to the directive. This includes national, regional, and local government agencies, and even EU institutions. ### 4. Others – “Supply‑Chain and Third‑Party Providers” NIS2 extends obligations to **suppliers and service providers** that deliver critical services or cybersecurity‑related products to the entities listed above. They must: * Conduct risk assessments. * Ensure that their own suppliers also meet security standards. * Report incidents that affect the essential/important entity. --- ## How the Directive is Implemented 1. **Member‑state transposition** * Each EU state must adopt national legislation that incorporates the directive’s requirements. * The law must define the set of entities, thresholds, and the supervisory authority. 2. **National Supervisory Authority (NSA)** * One or more bodies per member‑state that: * Oversees compliance. * Receives incident reports. * Conducts audits and enforcement actions. 3. **EU‑NIS‑CSIRT & EU‑NIS‑CSIRT Network** * Provides incident response support and threat intelligence sharing. 4. **Co‑operation** * Member‑states must cooperate via the **European Cybersecurity Coordination Group** (ECCC) and the **European Centre for the Protection of National Cybersecurity** (ENCS). --- ## Key Obligations for Entities | Obligation | What it entails | |------------|-----------------| | **Risk management** | Identify cyber risks, implement technical and organisational measures, maintain an incident response plan. | | **Incident reporting** | Notify the NSA within **24 hours** of a “security incident” that affects the continuity of the service. | | **Supply‑chain security** | Conduct security assessments of suppliers, require contractual security clauses. | | **Penalties** | Potential fines up to **€10 million** or **2 % of annual global turnover** (whichever is higher). | | **Information sharing** | Share relevant threat intelligence and incident data with EU‑NIS‑CSIRT and national CSIRTs. | --- ## Practical Take‑Home Messages | Who is it for? | What you must do? | |----------------|-------------------| | **Large companies** (energy, transport, finance, health, cloud, data centres) | Implement robust cyber‑security policies, report incidents quickly, conduct risk assessments. | | **Medium‑size digital platforms** (online marketplaces, social media, SaaS) | Meet reporting thresholds, adopt supply‑chain controls, cooperate with national authorities. | | **Small businesses** | If you provide essential services (e.g., a small water supplier), you still must comply—risk‑management, incident reporting. | | **Non‑EU providers** | If you serve EU customers and your service meets thresholds, you fall under NIS2 and must comply. | | **Suppliers & contractors** | Provide evidence of your own security controls; you may be audited by the entity you serve. | > **Bottom line:** If you operate a digital service that touches a large portion of EU users, or you provide a core service to the EU economy, you are **likely subject to NIS2**. Even if you’re a small company, you can’t ignore it if you fit any of the essential or important criteria. --- ## Resources for More Detail | Resource | What it offers | |----------|----------------| | **European Commission NIS2 Portal** | Full text of the directive, FAQs, implementation guidance. | | **European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA)** | Practical guidelines, risk assessment templates, case studies. | | **Your national NSA website** | National transposition laws, reporting portals, contact details. | | **Industry‑specific advisory groups** (e.g., ENERGY‑Securities, Cloud‑Security Alliance) | Tailored compliance checklists. | --- ### Bottom Line NIS2 is a **EU‑wide, high‑level cybersecurity framework** that expands the scope beyond the original NIS Directive to cover both essential and important services, including the largest digital platforms. If you run or supply a service that meets any of the defined thresholds, you must implement robust cyber‑risk management, report incidents within 24 hours, and cooperate with national and EU‑level authorities. The directive will be in force in all EU member‑states by **Feb 2025** (with a 6‑month grace period for the last‑minute adjustments), so it’s time to audit your current cyber‑security posture and start aligning with NIS2.
